newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin discusses NATO, March summit with Primakov.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin discusses NATO, March summit with Primakov.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin met his foreign minister Yevgeny Primakov on Sunday to discuss Moscow's relations with NATO and the Russian leader's planned summit later this month with U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Primakov also briefed Yeltsin on the results of his recent tour of several European capitals where NATO's plans to expand eastwards dominated the agenda, the presidential press service said in a statement.

Primakov, who met Yeltsin at the Gorky-9 residence outside Moscow where the president has been recovering from heart surgery and pneumonia, said he had made some progress in his talks with European officials.
"But negotiations with NATO are not like travelling along a wide avenue," the statement quoted Primakov as telling Yeltsin.
Russia remains firmly opposed to NATO's plans to offer membership to several former Warsaw Pact countries this summer, saying they represent a threat to its own security.
Negotiations are now focused on a document that will govern post-Cold War ties between the Atlantic alliance and Moscow.

Moscow wants the document to be legally binding and to contain commitments that NATO's military infrastructure will not be moved eastwards but the alliance favours a more flexible approach, saying a treaty would be unwieldy and take months to pass through national legislatures.
"The most important thing is that this document, which must have a binding character, would remove the grounds for Russia's fundamental concern," Sunday's press statement said.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, who plans to visit Moscow next weekend, said on Friday a mutually acceptable text could be ready for signing by the time of a July summit in Madrid at which NATO will invite new members to join.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are the favourites with Slovenia and Romania making strong last-minute pushes.
The issue of NATO expansion is expected to top the agenda of the U.S.-Russian summit in Helsinki on March 20 to 21.
On Sunday Yeltsin asked Primakov to make a working visit to the United States in the near future to complete preparations for the Helsinki summit.

During their discussions, Yeltsin and Primakov also touched on Russia's relations with other major nations and on the foreign affairs aspect of the president's annual address to parliament, which he will make on March 6.

The address and his meeting with Clinton two weeks later will mark Yeltsin's full return to political life after months of illness. He had open heart surgery last November and shortly after recovering from his operation went down with pneumonia.
